Data systems · Research note 03

From grid data to useful decisions

A power-data platform becomes valuable when it makes the data lineage, system context, and limits of its forecasts as visible as the charts themselves.

By Md Mahmud Akon5 min read · October 2026

National-grid data can answer practical questions: How does demand change through the day? Which generation sources respond to peaks? When do recurring patterns break? The first challenge, however, is rarely the forecasting model. It is creating a reliable path from scattered records to a consistent and inspectable dataset.

In developing the PGCB Power Data Visualizer, I treated collection, cleaning, visualization, and forecasting as one connected workflow. A polished chart built on inconsistent timestamps or silent missing values can communicate false confidence. Good presentation begins with explicit data handling.

Context before prediction

A useful dashboard should let a visitor understand recent history before presenting a forecast. Demand curves, fuel-mix changes, daily peaks, and gaps in the record all provide context. Forecasts become easier to judge when users can compare them with familiar patterns and recent deviations.

The goal of visualization is not to make uncertainty disappear. It is to make the evidence—and its limits—easier to inspect.

Forecasts need honest baselines

A 24-hour forecast should be compared with simple alternatives such as the previous day or a recent average. Evaluation should preserve time order and report performance across different periods, not only one favorable window. This keeps model complexity connected to measurable benefit.

Fuel-mix forecasting adds another layer: outputs are coupled because the components contribute to a total. A good interface can expose both the system-level curve and the contribution of each source without overwhelming the reader.

Product principle: every transformation—from source record to displayed value—should be reproducible, and every model output should be visually distinguishable from observation.

An open platform as a research tool

Beyond public communication, an open data platform creates a foundation for experiments in anomaly detection, renewable forecasting, demand response, and planning. It also reveals the practical limits of available data, which can be as informative as a benchmark score.

For me, that is the most interesting outcome: a software project that makes the grid easier to see while creating better questions for future energy research.
